claim.why_it_matters: Sibling clauses at the same numeric depth are transcribed at different markdown heading levels, so the outline/TOC nesting is wrong: D.14.3.2.3 renders as a peer of D.14.3.2 instead of a child of it, and D.14.3.3 as a peer of D.14.3 instead of a child. Any tool that derives clause structure (TOC, anchor generation, citation depth) from heading level mis-parents these clauses. The same defect recurs in this batch at '## D.14.3.4' (p1117), '## D.14.3.5' and '## D.14.3.6' (p1118), '## D.14.4' (p1119) and '## D.16.5' (p1124); the pattern across the whole file is that only the FIRST subclause under a parent keeps its correct level and every later sibling is promoted to '##' (specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 44889, 44898, 44949, 44999, 45024, 45047, 45179).

verdict.reasoning:
REJECTED. No content is missing or altered on page 1116, and the claim's own account of the defect is factually wrong in two places.

(1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The claim is filed as kind=missing-heading, but both headings are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md verbatim, in the right order, on the right page: line 44889 '## D.14.3.2.3 Switching locales outside of COBOL' and line 44898 '## D.14.3.3 Locale-based monetary and numeric formatting'. Clause numbers, titles, punctuation and the full body prose of both clauses (the SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO USER-DEFAULT example, the PICTURE +$9.9 LOCALE SIZE IS 10 examples, the SPECIAL-NAMES my-locale fragment) all match the rendered page exactly. The rejection criterion 'the missing text is actually present' fires directly.

(2) THE PDF CARRIES NO PRINTED DEPTH CUE, so nothing typographic was lost. I dumped the PDF text layer with PyMuPDF. Every clause heading in Annex D is set in the SAME font at the SAME size at the SAME left margin regardless of depth: Cambria,Bold 11.67pt at x0=63.5 for D.14 (2 components), D.14.1, D.14.2 (3), D.14.2.1, D.14.2.2 (4), and for both p1116 headings D.14.3.2.3 (5, y0=128.1) and D.14.3.3 (4, y0=267.2). The rendered 300dpi images of pp.1112/1114/1116 confirm this visually. The claim's phrase 'both printed at the same clause depth as their siblings' describes the NUMBERING, not anything the page prints; the PDF prints no level distinction at all. The only depth encoding on the printed page is the dotted-decimal number itself, and that is transcribed losslessly ('D.14.3.2.3' -> depth 5 deterministically). Zero information present in the PDF is absent from the markdown.

(3) THE CLAIMED PATTERN IS FALSE. The claim asserts 'only the FIRST subclause under a parent keeps its correct level and every later sibling is promoted to ##'. Refuted by the same batch: on p1121 D.16.1, D.16.2, D.16.3 AND D.16.4 are all '###' -- four consecutive siblings, every one keeping its level. The real mechanism is page-scoped level assignment: within each transcribed page the shallowest heading is emitted as '##' and deeper headings on that same page get '###'/'####', so the level resets at every page boundary. D.14.3.3 is '##' not because it is a 'later sibling' but because the page's first heading (D.14.3.2.3) already consumed '##' and D.14.3.3 is shallower than it. That makes this a global property of the transcription pipeline that would fire on hundreds of pages, not a page-1116 discrepancy.

(4) WHAT IS TRUE, AND WHY IT STILL DOES NOT QUALIFY. The observable inconsistency is real: numeric siblings do carry different '#' counts (D.14.3.2.1/.2 are '###' while D.14.3.2.3 is '##'; D.14.3.1 is '###' while D.14.3.3 is '##'), and this does diverge from the PDF's own bookmark tree, which assigns D.14.3.2.3 level 5 and D.14.3.3 level 4. But this is markdown heading formatting over text that is fully present, it changes no meaning, it loses no fact recoverable from the page, and the depth remains exactly derivable from the clause number -- which is the citation form this project actually uses. Both explicit rejection criteria ('the difference is only ... formatting' and 'the difference does not change meaning') apply. Annex D is informative, and no normative or informative statement is affected.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a page-1116 PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Both headings are transcribed verbatim with correct numbers, titles and body text; the PDF prints all Annex D clause headings identically (Cambria,Bold 11.67pt, x0=63.5) with no depth cue, so nothing was lost. The residual observation -- that markdown '#' counts do not track clause depth, diverging from the PDF's bookmark tree (D.14.3.2.3 = level 5, D.14.3.3 = level 4) -- is a real but purely cosmetic property of the whole transcription, and the claim mis-states its cause: levels are assigned per page (shallowest heading on a page becomes '##', deeper ones nest below it) and reset at each page boundary, NOT 'only the first subclause keeps its level' -- disproved by D.16.1 through D.16.4 on p1121, which are all '###'. If tracked at all this belongs as a single global transcription-pipeline note, not as a per-page structural finding.
